Evidently, there is no standard procedure for etching and cleaning, but the overall workflow should adhere to something like the following: 1. Degrease 2. Etch 3. Rinse 4. Ultrasonic clean 5. Although most steps in this process are meant to clean surfaces by removing dust or organic contaminants from the machining process, the effect of the acid etch is to deburr and smooth roughly machined surfaces. An investigation by Juwen Wang as the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory demonstrates the effectiveness of etching for removing surface defects such as machining burrs, rough machining lines, and embedded particles.26 Examples of these defects are shown in Figure 13. This investigation found an optimal etching time of 30 sec. This provides enough time to debur and smooth the surface but avoids pitting related to longer etching times. An additional process, electropolishing, is common in niobium superconducting niobium cavities and achieves superior surface finishes as compared to chemical polishing processes27 However, it is less common on copper structures. The electropolishing of copper is a mature technology but there is no relevant literature available on the effect of electropolishing for copper cavities in high-gradient structures. However, it is possible that future research reveals a need to electropolish in addition to chemical cleaning. In this case, electropolishing can be accomplished with the addition of an electropolishing bath and a rinse tank. B.2.2 Layout Adequately cleaning high-gradient structures can be lengthy and may require a large number of processing steps, necessitating a proportionate number of tanks and rinse stations.
